tagline: Aspen forest, stored mountain water and Zion’s red and white backcountry
intro: The Kolob Reservoir Scenic Backway runs 45 miles between SR-14 east of Cedar City and SR-9. Visit Cedar City promotes the drive for its passage through thick aspen forest, grassy meadows and the red and white backcountry of Zion National Park. The tourism office lists 90 minutes for the route.

The reservoir took shape in 1956, when the Hurricane Canal Company and Washington Fields Canal Company built an earthen dam across Kolob Creek. Its purpose was flood control and irrigation storage. The Washington County Water Conservation District now owns and operates the dam and continued developing the reservoir and its recreational facilities through the 2000s. The dam is 67 feet high and stretches 686 feet along its crest, holding a reservoir with a maximum capacity of 6,914 acre-feet.

Begin off SR-14, five miles east of Cedar City, and follow the backway through aspen forest to Kolob Reservoir. Beyond the water, grassy meadows lead into Zion’s red and white backcountry on the way to SR-9. In that sandstone country, Northgate Peaks’ two summits are composed of white Navajo Sandstone, with cross-bedding resembling the patterns on Checkerboard Mesa. The southern approach to the reservoir is in Virgin, a town on SR-9 beside its namesake river.

moments.title: Kolob Reservoir
moments.text: Kolob Reservoir is mountain water held for work downstream: the dam stores Kolob Creek water for irrigation and flood control. The Hurricane Canal Company and Washington Fields Canal Company built the earthen structure in 1956. It stands 67 feet high, with a crest 686 feet long. The reservoir lies on Kolob Mountain. Private grazing land surrounds the water, and fences mark the private boundary along almost all its shores. The Washington County Water Conservation District now owns and operates the dam and continued developing the reservoir’s size and recreational facilities through the 2000s.

moments.title: Northgate Peaks
moments.text: Two white Navajo Sandstone summits form the Northgate Peaks in Zion National Park. Their rock shows cross-bedding like that seen on Checkerboard Mesa. The west summit reaches 7,267 feet, higher than the east summit at 7,159 feet. Their name refers to their position at the head of a difficult passageway. Runoff drains to North Creek, a tributary of the Virgin River. The U.S. Board on Geographic Names adopted the name in 1935; the peaks stand north of their nearest higher neighbor, North Guardian Angel.

moments.title: Virgin
moments.text: Virgin takes its name from the river beside it and lies on SR-9 at 3,606 feet. The James Jepson Jr. House connects Virgin to another irrigation project. Jepson built the two-story limestone house in 1877 and is credited with the inception and construction of the Hurricane Canal. He lived there with his wife Lucinda Stratton and their children. The house entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2000.

practical: Kolob Reservoir: The backway closes in winter and is unsuitable for travel in wet conditions. (checked 2026-10-11)
